theme: I delight to do your will, the Son’s voice
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 40:1-10 and then glance at Hebrews 10:5-10 where this psalm is quoted. The psalm is David’s, but Hebrews hears it as the voice of the Son speaking to the Father. Read it twice, once as David’s testimony and once as Christ’s.
settingTheScene: In Hebrews 2 and 10, the author puts Old Testament psalms into the mouth of Jesus, treating them as the speech of the Son to the Father. Psalm 40 is one of these. In its original setting, David gives thanks for rescue from a pit and declares his joy in doing the will of God rather than offering mere sacrifices. Hebrews will take verses 6-8 and show that they find their fullest meaning in Christ, who came into the world to do the Father’s will by offering his own body. Today we read the psalm ahead of that application, so we are ready to hear it when we get there.
observation: David waited patiently for the LORD, and the LORD “inclined to me and heard my cry” (v. 1).
God lifted him from a “pit of destruction” and “the miry bog” and set his feet on a rock (v. 2).
God put “a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God” (v. 3).
Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD (v. 3).
“Sacrifice and offering you have not desired, but you have given me an open ear” (v. 6).
“Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me’” (v. 7).
“I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (v. 8).
David has told the glad news of deliverance “in the great congregation” and has not restrained his lips (vv. 9-10).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a testimony. David was in a pit, a place of helplessness, and he waited. The word suggests a long wait, and he does not complain but credits the LORD for hearing. The rescue is complete: the pit is replaced with a rock, and the mud with firm ground. And a new song fills his mouth. Rescue always produces praise.

Notice what happens next. David does not pretend that he can repay God. In verse 6, he says something surprising: “Sacrifice and offering you have not desired.” This was not a rejection of the sacrificial system, which God himself instituted, but a reminder that the sacrifices were never the point. What God wanted was an obedient heart. “You have given me an open ear.” The phrase may refer to a servant who willingly listens to his master. God wants those who hear him and respond.

Then David says, “Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me.” In David’s setting, this likely refers to the king’s duty described in the law (Deuteronomy 17:18-20). But Hebrews 10 reads it as the voice of Christ. When the Son came into the world, he said, “a body have you prepared for me” (the Greek translation of verse 6 that Hebrews quotes). The animal sacrifices could not take away sins. So Christ came, and he said: “I have come to do your will, O God.” By that will, we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

This is how the New Testament reads the Old. David’s experience is real, but it is also a shadow. His delight in doing God’s will is a faint picture of the perfect delight of the Son. His rescue from the pit is a hint of the great rescue from the grave. His proclamation in the great congregation looks ahead to the gospel going to the nations.

The last verses make an important point about testimony. David does not hide his deliverance. He proclaims God’s faithfulness and salvation and does not conceal his steadfast love. We are rescued so that others will see and trust.
connection: Psalm 40:6-8 is quoted in Hebrews 10:5-7 and is the voice of Christ as he comes into the world. The “open ear” recalls Isaiah 50:4-5, the Servant who listens and does not turn back. The rescue from the pit resonates with Joseph in Genesis 37, Jonah 2, and Psalm 30. The priority of obedience over sacrifice appears in 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalm 51:16-17, and Micah 6:6-8. “I delight to do your will” is the heart of Jesus’ own words in John 4:34 and Matthew 26:39.
application:
Think about the pit you have been rescued from. It may be sin, shame, fear, or something else. Write a short testimony of what God did, even just a few sentences. David did not hide his story, and your story may be what someone else needs to hear.

Examine your sense of delight. Do you obey God out of duty only, or is there any joy in it? Ask the Lord for the heart of the psalm: “your law is within my heart.” It is a gift, and Christ has given you his Spirit to produce it.

Finally, thank Jesus for saying what you could not say. He came to do the Father’s will. Because he did, you are free to approach.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for drawing you out of the pit and putting a new song in your mouth.
Thank him for the Son who came to do his will.
Ask him to give you delight in doing it.
